titre: Piper Alpha (1988): Cullen Moves Safety From Rule to Proof
accroche: After the 167 deaths on Piper Alpha, the Cullen report and then the 1992 regulations make every operator prove that its risks are under control.
contenu_vulgarise:
On the night of July 6, 1988, the oil platform Piper Alpha, in the North Sea, explodes and burns. There are 226 people on board. The toll is 167 dead. The immediate cause lies in a maintenance error: a pump was put back into service when its safety valve had been removed and replaced by a poorly tightened blind flange. But that is not what changes British regulation.

## What Lord Cullen Found

A public inquiry is entrusted to Lord Cullen. Its preliminary hearing is held on November 11, 1988; the public hearings proper open on January 19, 1989, and continue until February 15, 1990, in Aberdeen. The report is delivered in November 1990 and makes 106 recommendations, which the government and the industry implement, notably through the Offshore Safety Act 1992. The main one is not about a piece of metal. It concerns the way safety is regulated: offshore legislation was mostly prescriptive. The report leads to a regime in which those who create the risk must answer for how they guarantee safety, and not the State. The operator must demonstrate, for each of its installations, that the risks of a major accident are identified and under control. This document has a name: the “safety case.”

## From Rule to Demonstration

The 1992 regulations on offshore safety cases (Offshore Installations (Safety Case) Regulations 1992), made in November 1992 and applied from May 31, 1993, implement part of the report's main recommendations. They require the operator of a fixed installation or the owner of a mobile installation in British waters to submit to the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) a case, for each of its installations, containing what is needed to establish that its safety management systems are adequate and that the risks of major accidents to personnel are reduced to the lowest level reasonably practicable. Responsibility for offshore safety is also transferred from the Department of Energy to the HSE. An evaluation published by the HSE describes the result as the development of an approach based on goals rather than prescriptions: the State says where one must arrive, and the operator demonstrates how it gets there.

## The Shift

A catastrophe often produces more rules. Here, it also changed their nature: the safety case does not say which valve to install; it requires proof that the safety management systems are adequate. The change was not painless: the same evaluation notes, among the problems raised by the managers interviewed, the paperwork burden, an overload of texts (other regulations, including the one on fire and explosion prevention, complete the regime), and the fear of a return to prescription. A rule that asks for proof always needs someone willing to read it.

repere.texte: The Piper Alpha disaster, which occurred on July 6, 1988, killed 167 people and destroyed a major North Sea oil platform.
repere.source: Health and Safety Executive, evaluation of the offshore regulations (Safety Case Regulations 1992), introduction

carte.punch: After Piper Alpha, British offshore moves from prescription to proof.
carte.idee: After the Cullen report (1990) on Piper Alpha, 167 dead in 1988, the 1992 regulations require every British offshore operator to demonstrate, in a “safety case” submitted to the HSE, that its major risks are under control.

quiz.question: What do the 1992 regulations, made following the Cullen report, require of every British offshore operator?
choix: To apply a single list of technical prescriptions, set by the HSE for all platforms
To have each platform certified by a private insurer, in place of the HSE
To submit to the HSE a case demonstrating that the installation's major risks are under control
To shut down any installation over twenty years old until a new report is delivered
quiz.explication: The 1992 regulations require a safety case per installation, which the HSE assesses before accepting it: it is for the operator to demonstrate, and not for the State to prescribe each measure. No insurer takes the HSE's place, and the regime does not rest on a single list of prescriptions.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What must the safety case submitted to the HSE establish?
choix: That safety management systems are adequate and that major risks to personnel are reduced to the lowest level reasonably practicable
That the installation has had no notable accident or incident since its last HSE inspection
That the operator has set aside enough funds to compensate all victims of a possible major accident
That the installation complies with a fixed list of construction standards approved by the Department of Energy, with no further demonstration
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to the HSE evaluation, the case must demonstrate that adequate safety management systems are in place and that the risks of major accidents to personnel are reduced to the lowest level reasonably practicable. It is not limited to an accident history, a financial provision, or a list of standards.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which authority receives the safety cases of British offshore operators?
choix: The Department of Energy, which oversaw offshore safety before the reform
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Operators submit their case to the Health and Safety Executive, to which oversight of offshore safety was transferred from the Department of Energy.
